set.stem: A 74-year-old woman has progressive exertional breathlessness, angina and presyncope on climbing stairs. BP 138/76 mmHg, HR 78/min. There is a harsh late-peaking ejection systolic murmur at the right upper sternal edge, a soft S2 and a slow-rising (parvus et tardus) carotid pulse. Echocardiography: aortic valve area 0.8 cm², peak velocity 4.4 m/s, mean gradient 48 mmHg, LVEF 42% and moderate concentric LV hypertrophy. What is the best next step?
options: Elective surgical or transcatheter aortic valve replacement
Medical treatment and repeat echocardiography in 6–12 months
set.explanation: This is symptomatic severe aortic stenosis (valve area under 1.0 cm², mean gradient 40 mmHg or more, peak velocity 4 m/s or more) with LV systolic dysfunction; symptoms and an LVEF below 50% are each class I indications for aortic valve replacement. The heart team chooses between surgical AVR and TAVI (TAVI is generally favoured from about 75 years or with high surgical risk). No drug improves the outlook in severe AS: vasodilators and high-dose beta-blockers can precipitate hypotension, surveillance risks sudden death, and exercise testing is contraindicated in symptomatic severe AS (dobutamine stress echo is reserved for low-gradient AS with reduced EF).

why: The source values (mean gradient 34 mmHg with EF 42%) described low-flow low-gradient AS, for which stress echocardiography would be correct; velocity and gradient changed to unequivocally severe values

set.stem: A 36-year-old woman has exertional breathlessness and palpitations. There is a loud S1 and a low-pitched rumbling mid-diastolic murmur at the apex, best heard with the bell in the left lateral position and accentuated by brief exercise. Which additional finding most strongly supports mitral stenosis?
set.explanation: An opening snap – a sharp, high-pitched early diastolic sound after S2 as the stiff but still mobile rheumatic leaflets open – followed by a low-pitched mid-diastolic rumble with a loud S1 is characteristic of mitral stenosis; the shorter the S2 to opening snap interval, the more severe the stenosis. A soft S1 with an apical pansystolic murmur indicates mitral regurgitation, wide fixed splitting of S2 an atrial septal defect, an early diastolic decrescendo murmur at the left sternal edge aortic regurgitation, and a continuous murmur a PDA or arteriovenous fistula.

why: Removed the 'early diastolic sound' from the stem, which described the opening snap and gave away the answer

set.stem: A young woman has breathlessness and palpitations, and an early diastolic murmur is heard at the left sternal edge. Aortic regurgitation is suspected. Which finding argues AGAINST this diagnosis?
options: To-and-fro femoral bruit on compression (Duroziez sign)
Soft mid-diastolic murmur at the apex (Austin Flint murmur)
set.explanation: In significant chronic aortic regurgitation a large stroke volume is ejected and then runs back into the LV in diastole, giving a high systolic and low diastolic pressure – a wide pulse pressure. A BP of 120/95 mmHg (pulse pressure 25 mmHg with a high diastolic pressure) therefore argues against significant AR. The collapsing pulse, Duroziez and Quincke signs, head nodding (de Musset) and the Austin Flint murmur (the regurgitant jet impeding opening of the anterior mitral leaflet) all reflect a large regurgitant volume; in acute AR, however, the pulse pressure may be near normal.

why: Distractors of the duplicate 39 Blocks questions (valv-0005, valv-0008) merged into five options; key unchanged

set.explanation: Exertional and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea with basal crackles (left heart failure) and an apical pansystolic murmur radiating to the axilla is mitral regurgitation; in a young adult, rheumatic disease or mitral valve prolapse is the likely cause. Aortic stenosis gives an ejection systolic murmur at the right upper sternal edge radiating to the carotids, HCM an ejection systolic murmur at the left sternal edge that increases with Valsalva, and tricuspid regurgitation a pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge that increases on inspiration, with a raised JVP and large v waves. Echocardiography confirms the mechanism and severity.

why: Same idea as valv-0003 (a narrow pulse pressure is against aortic regurgitation); its Austin Flint distractor has been merged into valv-0003

set.stem: An elderly man with hypertension treated with lisinopril has exertional breathlessness. BP is 165/55 mmHg. There is a grade 2/6 early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge and a low-pitched mid-diastolic rumble at the apex; S1 is normal and there is no opening snap. What is the diagnosis?
set.explanation: An early diastolic decrescendo murmur at the left sternal edge with a wide pulse pressure is aortic regurgitation, and the apical mid-diastolic rumble is the Austin Flint murmur – the regurgitant jet striking the anterior mitral leaflet and causing functional obstruction to mitral inflow. It is distinguished from mitral stenosis by the normal S1, the absence of an opening snap and the accompanying signs of AR. Aortic stenosis and mitral regurgitation cause systolic murmurs; hypertension-related aortic root dilatation is a common cause of AR in older patients.

why: Removed the garbled '(and possibly previous syncope)'; added a wide pulse pressure, normal S1 and no opening snap to separate an Austin Flint murmur from mitral stenosis

set.stem: A 32-year-old woman with rheumatic heart disease for 20 years has breathlessness and fatigue. There is a soft S1, a loud S3 and an apical pansystolic murmur radiating to the axilla. Which investigation will NOT help in the diagnosis of her valve lesion?
set.explanation: The findings indicate chronic rheumatic mitral regurgitation (soft S1; S3 from rapid filling of a volume-loaded LV). Transthoracic and transoesophageal echocardiography with Doppler define the mechanism, severity, LV size and function, and cardiac catheterisation with left ventriculography can quantify the regurgitation and pressures when echo is inconclusive (coronary angiography is also done before surgery). Cardiac enzymes such as troponin and CK-MB detect myocardial necrosis and give no information about a chronic valve lesion.

why: Same idea as valv-0003 (a high diastolic pressure with a narrow pulse pressure is against aortic regurgitation)

set.stem: A patient has breathlessness, fatigue and leg oedema. There is a raised JVP with large v waves, a left parasternal (right ventricular) heave, a loud P2 and a pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge. Echocardiography shows right ventricular hypertrophy with structurally normal tricuspid leaflets and functional tricuspid regurgitation. What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
set.explanation: A loud P2, an RV heave and RV hypertrophy indicate raised pulmonary artery pressure; the tricuspid regurgitation is functional, caused by RV and annular dilatation, so the underlying diagnosis is pulmonary hypertension with right heart failure. Primary tricuspid disease (endocarditis, carcinoid, rheumatic disease, Ebstein anomaly) shows abnormal leaflets and does not cause a loud P2 or RV hypertrophy. Pulmonary regurgitation gives an early diastolic (Graham Steell) murmur, and dilated cardiomyopathy predominantly affects the LV. The next step is to identify the cause: left heart disease, lung disease, chronic thromboembolism or pulmonary arterial hypertension.

why: The option 'tricuspid regurgitation' was itself the echo finding; stem and options reworded so the question asks for the underlying cause

set.stem: A 71-year-old man with rheumatic heart disease for 20 years presents with breathlessness on exertion. BP is 128/78 mmHg. On examination the apex beat is displaced, the first heart sound is soft and the second heart sound is normal. Which valvular lesion is most likely?
set.explanation: A displaced (volume-loaded) apex with a soft S1 in rheumatic heart disease indicates mitral regurgitation: incomplete leaflet coaptation softens S1 and the LV dilates to accommodate the regurgitant volume; an apical pansystolic murmur radiating to the axilla and an S3 would be expected. Mitral stenosis gives a loud S1, opening snap and a tapping undisplaced apex, aortic stenosis a heaving but usually undisplaced apex with a soft S2, and aortic regurgitation also displaces the apex but causes a wide pulse pressure and an early diastolic murmur.

why: Added a normal blood pressure/pulse pressure to exclude aortic regurgitation, which can also give a displaced apex
Same idea as valv-0022 (mid-diastolic rumble with opening snap/loud S1 = mitral stenosis); valv-0011 also misplaced the murmur at the left sternal edge
Same idea as valv-0006 (early diastolic murmur = aortic regurgitation)

set.stem: A 62-year-old woman with known rheumatic mitral stenosis presents with progressive breathlessness, ankle swelling and abdominal distension. She is in sinus rhythm. Examination shows a raised JVP, a left parasternal heave, tender hepatomegaly and pitting oedema to the knees. What is the most likely cause of her new symptoms?
options: Progression to pulmonary hypertension with right heart failure
set.explanation: Long-standing mitral stenosis raises left atrial and pulmonary venous pressure; with time, reactive pulmonary arteriolar constriction and remodelling cause pulmonary hypertension and the right ventricle fails, giving a raised JVP, RV heave, hepatomegaly and oedema, often with functional tricuspid regurgitation. AF is the commonest trigger of acute decompensation in MS but is excluded here by sinus rhythm; MR would add an apical pansystolic murmur and LV dilatation, and nothing suggests infarction or effusion. Symptomatic severe MS with pulmonary hypertension is an indication for balloon valvotomy or valve surgery.

why: The source stem ('progressive dyspnoea and congestion') was equally consistent with new AF; sinus rhythm and right-heart-failure signs added

set.stem: What is the typical character of the apex beat in a patient with mitral stenosis?
set.explanation: In mitral stenosis the apex beat is undisplaced, because the LV is protected from volume and pressure overload, and tapping – a palpable loud S1 as the thickened leaflets close from a widely open position. A displaced forceful apex indicates LV volume overload (MR, AR), a heaving apex LV pressure overload (AS, hypertension), and a left parasternal heave in MS suggests RV hypertrophy from pulmonary hypertension.

set.stem: Which auscultatory finding most suggests pulmonary hypertension in a patient with mitral stenosis?
set.explanation: Pulmonary hypertension increases the force of pulmonary valve closure, giving a loud (sometimes palpable) P2, often with an RV heave, a raised JVP and functional tricuspid regurgitation or a Graham Steell murmur. The opening snap and loud S1 come from the stenotic mitral valve itself and do not reflect pulmonary pressure, a diminished S2 suggests aortic stenosis, and an ejection click suggests a bicuspid aortic or stenotic pulmonary valve.

set.stem: In which patient with mitral stenosis is percutaneous balloon mitral commissurotomy indicated?
set.explanation: Percutaneous mitral balloon commissurotomy is indicated in symptomatic, clinically significant MS (valve area 1.5 cm² or less) with favourable anatomy – pliable, non-calcified leaflets with little subvalvular disease – no more than mild MR and no left atrial thrombus on transoesophageal echocardiography. Heavy calcification, moderate or severe MR or LA thrombus favour surgical valve replacement. Selected asymptomatic patients at high risk (pulmonary hypertension, new AF, planned pregnancy) may also be treated; age and AF alone are not criteria.

set.stem: A 34-year-old woman with a past history of rheumatic fever presents with breathlessness on exertion and a malar flush. She is in sinus rhythm, and echocardiography confirms mitral stenosis. Which physical sign is she likely to have?
set.explanation: In mitral stenosis with sinus rhythm, atrial contraction at the end of diastole increases flow across the narrowed valve, producing pre-systolic accentuation of the mid-diastolic rumble; it disappears when AF develops. Other findings are a loud S1, an opening snap and a tapping undisplaced apex. An ejection systolic murmur suggests aortic or pulmonary outflow disease, a mid-systolic click mitral valve prolapse, a quiet S2 severe aortic stenosis, and a thrusting apex LV volume overload.

set.stem: An 80-year-old man is found to have an incidental ejection systolic murmur, and his family physician feels a systolic thrill at the base of the heart. What is the most likely cause of the thrill?
set.explanation: A thrill is a palpable murmur (grade 4/6 or louder); in an elderly man, a loud ejection systolic murmur with a thrill at the base (aortic area, suprasternal notch, carotids) is most likely calcific aortic stenosis, although loudness correlates poorly with severity and echocardiography is needed. An ASD produces a soft pulmonary flow murmur without a thrill, mitral stenosis a diastolic murmur, and pulmonary hypertension and RV hypertrophy a palpable P2 and a left parasternal heave rather than a thrill.

why: 'Parasternal thrill' (which suggests a VSD) changed to a thrill at the base of the heart, where the thrill of aortic stenosis is felt

set.stem: A 43-year-old man has a routine health check at work. He has a murmur, isolated systolic hypertension (180/60 mmHg) and left ventricular hypertrophy on his ECG. Echocardiography shows significant regurgitant flow across the aortic valve. Which clinical sign is he likely to have?
options: Head nodding in time with the heartbeat (de Musset sign)
set.explanation: A pulse pressure of 120 mmHg with LVH and significant aortic regurgitation indicates a large regurgitant volume, producing the hyperdynamic signs of AR: a collapsing (water-hammer) pulse, visible carotid pulsation (Corrigan sign), head nodding (de Musset sign), capillary pulsation (Quincke sign), pistol-shot femorals and Duroziez sign. An opening snap and tapping apex belong to mitral stenosis, a slow-rising pulse to aortic stenosis, and pulsus paradoxus to tamponade or severe asthma. Severe AR with LV dilatation or dysfunction is referred for valve surgery.

why: de Musset sign was mislabelled as neck pulsation (that is Corrigan sign); distractors replaced because an ejection systolic flow murmur, a thrill and a soft A2 can all occur in severe AR

set.stem: An 84-year-old woman with diabetes and hyperlipidaemia had an anterior STEMI 3 weeks ago, treated with primary PCI and a drug-eluting stent to the left anterior descending artery. She has been well since on metoprolol, aspirin, clopidogrel, rosuvastatin, lisinopril and insulin. Her ophthalmologist has scheduled elective cataract surgery for next week but considers the bleeding risk too high while she takes both antiplatelet drugs, and asks your advice. What should you recommend?
options: Stop aspirin, continue clopidogrel and proceed with surgery
Stop clopidogrel, continue aspirin and proceed with surgery
Stop both antiplatelet drugs and proceed with surgery
Postpone surgery for at least 6 months, preferably 12, when clopidogrel can be stopped
Proceed with surgery on both drugs, as she will never be able to stop either
set.explanation: After an ACS treated with a drug-eluting stent, dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin plus a P2Y12 inhibitor) is normally continued for 12 months, and stopping clopidogrel 3 weeks after stenting carries a high risk of stent thrombosis, which is often fatal. Elective surgery such as cataract extraction should therefore be deferred until the minimum DAPT period is complete (at least 6 months, ideally 12 after ACS), after which clopidogrel is stopped and aspirin continued lifelong. Aspirin should not be stopped in a patient with a coronary stent, and 'never stopping either' is wrong because the P2Y12 inhibitor has a defined duration; many surgeons will in fact operate on uninterrupted antiplatelets, as cataract surgery under topical anaesthesia has a low bleeding risk.

set.stem: An 87-year-old woman with severe COPD (FEV1 0.76 L), poorly controlled diabetes and stage 3 chronic kidney disease presents with exertional chest pressure, leg swelling, breathlessness and rapidly worsening fatigue. There is a harsh late-peaking systolic murmur at the right upper sternal edge radiating to the carotids, an inaudible S2 and slow-rising, delayed carotid pulses. Echocardiography confirms aortic stenosis with a valve area of 0.59 cm². The cardiothoracic surgeon declines surgical aortic valve replacement because her predicted in-hospital mortality exceeds 15%. Which statement to her is reasonable?
options: For this condition, medications have been shown to reduce the risk of death
It does not matter that you are not a surgical candidate: your condition carries a low 1- and 5-year mortality, and medication can control your symptoms
Percutaneous balloon aortic valvotomy is a good non-surgical option with excellent short- and long-term results
As you are not a surgical candidate, no other procedure can replace your valve, so we should consider hospice care
We should refer you for assessment for transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI)
set.explanation: Symptomatic severe AS carries a very poor prognosis without valve replacement (about 50% mortality within 2 years of symptom onset), and no drug alters its course. Transcatheter aortic valve implantation is the treatment of choice for patients at high or prohibitive surgical risk, and heart-team assessment (CT of the aortic root and iliofemoral access, frailty and comorbidity) decides candidacy. Balloon aortic valvotomy gives only transient benefit with early restenosis and is used as a bridge or palliation, and hospice care is appropriate only if TAVI is also judged futile.

set.stem: A 42-year-old man presents with shortness of breath and haemoptysis. On examination there is a loud first heart sound and a rumbling mid-diastolic murmur at the apex. What is the most likely diagnosis?
set.explanation: A loud S1 and a low-pitched rumbling mid-diastolic murmur at the apex are the hallmarks of mitral stenosis, usually rheumatic; there may also be an opening snap and, in sinus rhythm, pre-systolic accentuation. Haemoptysis results from raised pulmonary venous pressure (rupture of bronchial veins, pulmonary oedema or infarction). MR and AS cause systolic murmurs, AR an early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge, and tricuspid stenosis a mid-diastolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge that increases on inspiration.

why: Same idea as valv-0004 (apical pansystolic murmur radiating to the axilla = mitral regurgitation)

set.stem: A 62-year-old man presents with angina and breathlessness. On examination there is an ejection systolic murmur at the upper right sternal edge radiating to the neck. What is the most likely diagnosis?
set.explanation: An ejection systolic (crescendo–decrescendo) murmur at the upper right sternal edge radiating to the carotids is aortic stenosis; angina, exertional breathlessness and syncope are the classic symptoms and signal severe disease needing valve replacement. MR gives an apical pansystolic murmur radiating to the axilla, MS an apical mid-diastolic rumble, AR an early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge, and tricuspid stenosis a diastolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge.

why: Same idea as valv-0006 (early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge = aortic regurgitation)

set.stem: A 42-year-old man is reviewed in the cardiology clinic after an echocardiogram showing right ventricular dysfunction. He has a raised JVP and a pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge. What is the most likely diagnosis?
set.explanation: A pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge (louder on inspiration – Carvallo sign) with a raised JVP showing large v waves and RV dysfunction is tricuspid regurgitation, usually functional from RV dilatation (pulmonary hypertension, left heart disease) and sometimes primary (endocarditis in people who inject drugs, carcinoid, Ebstein anomaly). A pulsatile liver, ascites and oedema may follow. Mitral regurgitation is apical and radiates to the axilla, and the other lesions do not cause pansystolic murmurs.

set.stem: A 62-year-old man presents with angina and breathlessness. There is an ejection systolic murmur at the upper right sternal edge radiating to the neck. Which investigation is most likely to establish the diagnosis?
set.explanation: Transthoracic echocardiography with Doppler is the key investigation for any suspected valve lesion: it confirms aortic stenosis, grades its severity (peak velocity, mean gradient, valve area) and assesses LV hypertrophy and function, which determine the need for valve replacement. The ECG may show LVH and the chest X-ray a calcified valve or post-stenotic dilatation, but neither is diagnostic; coronary angiography is done before valve surgery to identify coexisting coronary disease, and a 24-hour ECG is for arrhythmias.

set.stem: A 42-year-old man presents with shortness of breath and haemoptysis. There is a loud first heart sound and a rumbling mid-diastolic murmur at the apex. An echocardiogram and chest X-ray are requested. All of the following are chest X-ray features of this condition EXCEPT:
set.explanation: In mitral stenosis the enlarged left atrium straightens the left heart border, produces a double right heart border and splays (widens, not narrows) the carina by elevating the left main bronchus. Pulmonary venous hypertension causes upper-lobe venous diversion and interstitial oedema with Kerley B lines, and pulmonary hypertension leads to enlarged pulmonary arteries and right-sided (including right atrial) enlargement; mitral valve calcification may also be seen.
